title: Foreign-currency borrowing would change how Sweden funds its reserves
summary: The Riksbank plans to borrow about SEK 200 billion in foreign currency through the Swedish National Debt Office. Its immediate concern is how much a stronger krona can erode the value of its balance sheet. The bank intends to preserve the reserve’s long-term size. The distinction matters for SEK investors: the announcement describes a series of future currency transactions in pursuit of a balance-sheet objective. It gives neither an exchange-rate target nor a judgement about where the policy rate should go.

The exposure follows from a financing decision in 2021. Under self-financing, the Riksbank holds foreign-currency assets against krona liabilities. An appreciation reduces the krona value of the assets while the krona amount owed stays the same. Funding part of the reserve in the currencies held brings an offsetting valuation change on the liability side. It would also allow the bank to retire FX swaps that it has used for hedging since 2023. Thus the headline SEK 200 billion covers both a change in the financing of existing assets and the replacement of an existing hedge. The release gives no split between the two.

The bank provisionally envisages starting in the first quarter of 2027 if market conditions remain stable, and taking 12 to 18 months to complete the operation. It expects to sell foreign currency for kronor and replace outstanding swaps. It intends to spread the transactions evenly to limit the impact on the exchange rate. Those qualifications matter for any near-term trading interpretation. The release establishes the direction of the planned currency sales, but supplies no dealing dates, currency-specific volumes or estimate of the price effect. The next identified occasion for implementation details is the December monetary policy decision.

The reserve was worth approximately SEK 450 billion at the end of October. It serves several purposes, including foreign-currency liquidity support for banks, capacity for intervention and Sweden’s obligations under the IMF’s Special Drawing Rights system. Keeping assets available for those purposes is compatible with reducing the currency risk borne by the Riksbank. The Debt Office would administer the borrowing. The release describes a statutory limit of 5% of GDP at the time of decision. That is a legal measure of borrowing capacity, distinct from the provisional SEK amount the bank intends to raise.

questions.question: How much of the transition would actually require outright krona purchases?
questions.detail: The announcement specifies two implementation legs. Their relative sizes determine how much new outright FX flow a dealer could expect. Read the accompanying Markets Department memorandum for the provisional split, then compare it with the implementation terms the Riksbank expects to give in December.

questions.question: Which currencies would see transactions, and at what pace?
questions.detail: An evenly spread programme still leaves uncertainty about the currency mix, the spacing of transactions and how operations would change if market conditions deteriorated. Check currency-level dealing terms, Debt Office borrowing announcements and published execution results before estimating monthly market exposure.

questions.question: How would the matched debt change the reserve’s usable liquidity?
questions.detail: The bank intends to preserve the long-term stock of reserve assets, while the new liabilities will have their own cash-flow dates. For a liquidity assessment, compare reserve maturity and currency disclosures with the Debt Office’s eventual funding and redemption schedule. The release contains no maturity ladder.
